title: When work acts: standing, scheduled, occasioned

answer.title: What kind of thing is it, by when it acts?
answer.lede: Two questions name it: what sets it off, and whether it acts once or each time from something written down. The right-hand column is what you call occasioned.

cells.means: goes off once, at a time set in advance
the clock sets off each run
kept in force: acts at each occasion until withdrawn
a clock repeats only from something written down
it comes again and again, and is decided each time

add.means: someone asks for each run of a kept procedure
it runs each time, but acts only when a check finds a reason

requires.gate: acts only if a check finds a reason

add.means: a timed check finds its occasion, so it acts at the next check
someone runs it to a calendar, from written steps

renames.why: No clock sets it off: it runs when a session starts, if two days have passed. The registry's README says a blank schedule means no schedule.
It runs when a view that reads it opens, and reads only repos that moved. app/index.html says its old interval was never a schedule.
docs/properties.csv files GitHub's schedule among the events, so the harness counts an hourly cron as event-fired.

web-tools calls a Claude scheduled task a Routine in writers.csv, venues.md, vocabularies.csv and inbound.md; the registry calls it a scheduled task, and budget-drs uses routine for work someone runs to a calendar.

open.question: Adopt occasioned for whatever the clock does not set off?
open.why: The scheduled-task registry already defines scheduled as neither someone asking nor something happening; occasioned names that half in one word. The only near use is the noun occasion, an approval field and a pub/sub tag.

open.question: What should a timer set to go off once be called?
open.why: The send-later guard already calls the kind someone asked for a reminder, and a standing instruction refuses the other kind, the PR check-in.

open.question: Retire triggered and periodic as words for when estate work acts?
open.why: Triggered means any start, an event or a condition by turns; periodic's one live use names a crawl that runs when a view opens. Say what sets it off, or say gated. The budget submittal's if-triggered status follows OFM's forms and can stay.

open.question: Keep news-fetch in the scheduled-task registry once it is not called scheduled?
open.why: Its timing matters, since feeds drop items after about three days, which is why it sits there; no clock sets it off, which is why the name is wrong.

answer.by: Reader T (skill), one run: 33 things in web-tools, home and web-tools-private, coded by hand on nine questions; the examples are placed by that coding.

steps.gloss: List each word and each way the files use it, with the line that uses it.
steps.example: Triggered is used three ways: any start, an event, and a condition a budget form waits on.

steps.gloss: Turn what the senses imply into questions with a fixed set of answers.
steps.example: Does the clock set it off? Does it act once, each time from something written down, or each time decided anew?

steps.gloss: Find what each word is applied to, add things no word is applied to, and answer every question for each.
steps.example: 33 things, from the morning brief to a recurring fork. news-fetch is called scheduled, but a session start sets it off.

steps.gloss: A script flags a question that tells nothing apart, things nothing tells apart, and a combination nothing has. Each flag is answered.
steps.example: Nothing separates /drain, the Standing loop and a prompt used ad hoc, so recurring, standing and ad hoc named one thing there.

steps.gloss: Say what kind of category each sense is, then draw the words onto the two questions that decide them.
steps.example: Scheduled and occasioned answer one question; one-off, standing and ad hoc answer the other.

runs.method: cat-map skill, one reader: senses read from the files, instances found by search in web-tools, home and web-tools-private, coded by hand

pairs.question: Both are an app's timed check. Scheduled or occasioned?
Both are rows of the scheduled-task registry. Is news-fetch scheduled?
Both are kept and act again and again. Is a skill standing, as a hook is?
One is refused and the other allowed. What separates them?
Both keep a calendar. Is the monthly report scheduled?
Both refresh caches. Is the config crawl periodic?
Both are one-off asks. Does the daemon's minute pass change what an errand is?

outcome.summary: A mix, mostly values on different axes. Scheduled and occasioned answer what sets it off. One-off, standing and ad hoc answer whether it acts once, each time from something written down, or each time decided anew, and recurring covers the last two. Periodic and the budget-drs routine add a calendar; the Claude Routine is a second name for scheduled. Triggered names the start question itself in one sense, an event in a second and a gate in a third.

findings.text: by_clock is fixed once set_off is known
findings.rationale: Kept both. Scheduled and occasioned are defined on by_clock alone, and a sense can require only one value, so occasioned cannot be stated on set_off; set_off splits the occasioned half into an event and an ask.

findings.text: occasions is fixed once pattern is known
findings.rationale: Kept both. Recurring means each time whether or not anything is written down, which pattern alone cannot state; pattern splits each time by whether it is written down, which is what separates standing from ad hoc.
Two plain scheduled tasks. They differ in the machine that runs them, the laptop daemon or GitHub, which no word under test is about.

findings.text: no characteristic separates pre-commit, news-fetch, submittal-note, config-crawl
findings.rationale: One kind of thing under four names: a kept mechanism that a commit, a session start or a view opening sets off, and that acts only when a check finds a reason. news-fetch is called scheduled and the config crawl periodic; both are renamed.
Called triggered and standing for the same values: an event sets off a kept mechanism each time. The two words name one answer here.
Two standing instructions, both called standing; nothing should separate them.

findings.text: no characteristic separates drain, standing-loop, spike-prompt, sweep
findings.rationale: Called recurring, standing, ad hoc and nothing for the same values: a kept procedure someone asks for each time. The answer gives all four one name, standing on request.
Two routines: someone runs each to a calendar from written steps. budget-drs calls one routine and the other recurring work.
Two polled one-offs. They differ in the agent that does the work, Gemini or Codex, which is not a when-question.

findings.text: no instance is each time, decided anew and yes
findings.rationale: Impossible: a clock fires again only from something written down, a cron row or a stored prompt, so nothing the clock sets off is decided anew each time.

findings.text: no instance is not fixed in advance and yes
findings.rationale: Impossible: a clock sets off work at a time set in advance, even when the run lands within the hour rather than at the minute.
